section: Educational Psychology · Ch12 — Special Needs & Inclusive Education
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A child of normal or above-average intelligence struggles specifically with reading — reversing letters, reading slowly, and mixing up similar-looking words — despite adequate instruction. This is most characteristic of:

options.option_text: Dyslexia
Intellectual disability
Autism Spectrum Disorder
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder

explanation: Dyslexia is a specific learning disability affecting reading, distinct from general intellectual disability — the child's overall intelligence is typically normal, and the difficulty is specific to decoding text.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch12 — Special Needs & Inclusive Education
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A pupil who struggles specifically with number concepts, arithmetic operations and understanding quantities, despite normal ability in reading, likely has:

options.option_text: Dyscalculia
Dyslexia
Dysgraphia
Aphasia

explanation: Dyscalculia specifically affects mathematical understanding; dyslexia affects reading; dysgraphia affects handwriting/written expression; aphasia is a language-production/comprehension impairment usually from brain injury.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch12 — Special Needs & Inclusive Education
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A child on the autism spectrum often benefits most from classroom strategies that provide:

options.option_text: Predictable routines, clear visual schedules and structured environments
Frequent, unannounced changes to the daily schedule
Constant loud group activities with no quiet space
Complete isolation from all classroom activities

explanation: Predictability and visual structure reduce anxiety and support learning for many children with ASD, who often find sudden change and sensory overload distressing — while still being included, not isolated, in the classroom.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch12 — Special Needs & Inclusive Education
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A gifted child who finishes assigned work quickly and becomes bored/disruptive is best supported by:

options.option_text: Enrichment activities and advanced challenges suited to their pace
Repeating the same-level work over and over
Punishing the child for finishing early
Ignoring the child's advanced ability entirely

explanation: Gifted learners need differentiated enrichment (deeper/broader challenges) to stay engaged — repetition of mastered work or ignoring their pace often leads to disengagement or behavioural issues, as seen here.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch12 — Special Needs & Inclusive Education
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: The key difference between mere 'integration' and true 'inclusion' of a child with disability in a mainstream school is that inclusion additionally requires:

options.option_text: Adapting the curriculum, teaching methods and environment to the child's needs, not just physical presence
Placing the child physically in the classroom with no other changes
Separating the child into a special classroom within the same building
Excluding the child from assessments entirely

explanation: Integration is often just physical placement in the mainstream setting; inclusion goes further, adapting curriculum, pedagogy and assessment so the child genuinely participates and learns — the more complete model.
